eras: Israel between Egypt and Canaan, as the Torah tells it
Tribes without a king, c. 1400–1050 BC
Saul, David, Solomon, then Israel and Judah, c. 1050–586 BC
Jerusalem destroyed, the people deported, 586–538 BC
A small province rebuilding Jerusalem, 538–400 BC
Small house churches across the Roman Empire, AD 48–67
Letters to a church under pressure
Christians facing suspicion and persecution, AD 60–100

GEN.to: Israel in the wilderness, a people just freed from slavery in Egypt
GEN.w: Every neighbouring nation had its own creation story and gods of sun, sea and storm. Genesis answers them: one God makes all of these, and humans, not kings alone, carry his image.
GEN.q: Many scholars date the final form of the Torah to the 500s–400s BC, drawing on older sources.

EXO.to: The generation that came out of Egypt
EXO.w: Egypt was the superpower of the age and Pharaoh was treated as a god. The story shows Israel's God defeating Egypt's gods and making a covenant like the treaties great kings made with lesser nations.
EXO.q: See Genesis on the dating of the Torah.

LEV.to: Priests and people camped around the tabernacle
LEV.w: Sacrifice was how every ancient people approached a god. Leviticus uses the shared language of offerings, purity and holy space but ties it to one God who lives among his people.
LEV.q: See Genesis on the dating of the Torah.

NUM.to: Israel's tribes on the forty-year march
NUM.w: Nomadic tribes counted fighting men and marched by clan. Numbers records the census, the camp order and the grumbling of a generation that did not enter the land.
NUM.q: See Genesis on the dating of the Torah.

DEU.to: The new generation on the plains of Moab, about to cross the Jordan
DEU.w: Its shape follows ancient Near Eastern vassal treaties: history, terms, blessings and curses, witnesses. Its first hearers would have recognised a covenant document.
DEU.q: Many scholars link it to King Josiah's reform in 622 BC (2 Kings 22).

JOS.w: Canaan was a patchwork of walled city-states, nominally under Egypt. Land was the gift that made Israel a nation.
JOS.q: Many scholars place its final form in the 600s–500s BC.

JDG.to: Israel in the time before the monarchy
JDG.w: No central government: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes." Philistines held the coast with iron weapons. The book argues that Israel needed faithful leadership.

RUT.d: Set in the judges' era, written c. 1000 BC or later
RUT.to: Israelites who knew David as king
RUT.w: A Moabite widow becomes David's great-grandmother. Moab was a hated enemy (Deuteronomy 23:3), so the story makes a pointed claim about who belongs.
RUT.q: Some date it after the exile, as a reply to Ezra's ban on foreign wives.

1SA.to: Israel asking why it has kings and why David's line
1SA.w: The tribes had just become a kingdom. Neighbouring kings claimed divine right. Samuel shows a king who must answer to a prophet.
1SA.q: Final form often dated to the exile, c. 560 BC.

2SA.w: Court history of David, told with his failures in plain view. Unusual among ancient royal records, which praised kings.
2SA.q: Final form often dated to the exile, c. 560 BC.

1KI.to: Exiles in Babylon asking why Jerusalem fell
1KI.w: Written after the end: the temple was ash and the king a prisoner. Every reign is judged by one test, faithfulness to God.

2KI.to: Exiles in Babylon asking why Jerusalem fell
2KI.w: Assyria destroyed the north in 722 BC, Babylon the south in 586 BC. The book ends with the exiled king released from prison, a thin thread of hope.

1CH.to: Jews back in a small Persian province
1CH.w: No king, a modest temple, Persian rule. Chronicles retells Israel's story through the temple and David's line to give the returned community its identity.

2CH.to: Jews back in a small Persian province
2CH.w: It ends with Cyrus of Persia ordering the temple rebuilt, the very hope its readers were living in.

EZR.w: Persia let subject peoples keep their gods and laws. Ezra quotes Persian decrees, partly in Aramaic, the empire's official language.

NEH.w: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king. Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins and neighbouring governors opposed rebuilding them.

EST.to: Jews scattered across the Persian Empire
EST.w: Most Jews never returned. Esther tells of survival in the Persian court at Susa, and God is never named in the Hebrew text.

JOB.d: Unknown; set in the age of the patriarchs
JOB.to: Readers wrestling with why the righteous suffer
JOB.w: Ancient wisdom held that the good prosper and the wicked fall. Job takes on that belief head-on.
JOB.q: Dates proposed range from 1000 to 400 BC.

PSA.by: David, Asaph, the sons of Korah and others
PSA.to: Worshippers at the temple, then exiles and returnees
PSA.w: Israel's hymnbook. Songs for kings, pilgrims and laments over Jerusalem sit side by side. Book 5 was finished after the exile.

PRO.to: Young men being trained for court and household
PRO.w: Wisdom schools in Egypt and Mesopotamia wrote similar sayings. One section (22:17–24:22) closely parallels the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

ECC.to: Thoughtful readers asking what life under the sun amounts to
ECC.w: A rich king's experiment with every pleasure and project, ending in fear of God.
ECC.q: Its late Hebrew leads many scholars to date it c. 300–200 BC.

SNG.w: Love songs were common across the ancient world, especially in Egypt. Jewish and Christian readers also took it as a picture of God and his people.

ISA.w: Assyria was swallowing nations whole. Isaiah warned kings not to trust alliances with Egypt.
ISA.q: Many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to prophets during and after the exile.

JER.to: Jerusalem in its last decades, then the first exiles
JER.w: Babylon had replaced Assyria. Jeremiah told Judah to submit, which got him called a traitor.

LAM.w: Five funeral poems for a city. Four are acrostics, one verse per letter of the alphabet.

EZK.w: Exiles living by the river Chebar. Ezekiel shows God's glory leaving the temple and promises it will return.

DAN.w: Captives trained in the Babylonian court. Visions of four empires that pass away before God's kingdom.
DAN.q: Most critical scholars date its final form to c. 165 BC, under the persecution of Antiochus IV.

HOS.w: Prosperity and Baal worship before Assyria's attack. Hosea's broken marriage pictures Israel's unfaithfulness.

JOL.w: A locust swarm becomes a picture of the coming day of the Lord.
JOL.q: Proposed dates range from c. 800 BC to after the exile, c. 400 BC.

AMO.to: The wealthy northern kingdom of Israel
AMO.w: Peace and luxury for the rich, injustice for the poor. A southern farmer preaches in the north's royal shrine.

OBA.w: Edom, Israel's kin nation, joined in looting Jerusalem in 586 BC.

JON.w: Nineveh was the capital of Israel's cruellest enemy. That God spares it is the sting of the book.
JON.q: Many date the writing after the exile.

MIC.w: Contemporary of Isaiah. Speaks for villagers whose land was taken by the rich.

NAM.w: A poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh, which happened in 612 BC.

HAB.w: Why would God use a crueller nation to punish Judah? "The just shall live by his faith."

ZEP.w: Before Josiah's reform, Baal and star worship filled Jerusalem.

HAG.to: Returnees who had stopped rebuilding the temple
HAG.w: Fifteen years after the return the temple was still a foundation. Bad harvests, and Persian politics in turmoil.

ZEC.w: Night visions encouraging the governor Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua.

MAL.w: The temple stood, but priests offered lame animals and tithes went unpaid.

MAT.w: Written for readers who knew the Hebrew Scriptures. It keeps saying "that it might be fulfilled" and presents Jesus as a new Moses.

MRK.by: John Mark (by tradition), from Peter's preaching
MRK.w: Mark explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words. Rome's Christians had just faced Nero's persecution.

LUK.by: Luke, a physician and companion of Paul
LUK.w: Opens like a Greek history. Emphasises the poor, women and outsiders.

JHN.to: Churches in Asia Minor, around Ephesus
JHN.w: Written as synagogues and churches were parting ways. Uses Greek ideas like the Logos, the Word.

ACT.to: Theophilus, and the wider Greek-speaking world
ACT.w: Traces the message from Jerusalem to Rome and repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Christians innocent.

ROM.to: Jewish and Gentile Christians in Rome
ROM.w: Emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome in AD 49. When they returned the church was mixed and divided.

1CO.w: Corinth was a rich, rebuilt Roman port with dozens of temples. Its church brought the city's status-seeking, lawsuits and banquets with it.

2CO.w: Rival teachers had come with letters of recommendation and polished speech. Paul defends his weakness.

GAL.to: Churches in the Roman province of Galatia
GAL.w: Teachers were telling Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

EPH.w: Ephesus was home to the great temple of Artemis and a busy trade in magic.

PHP.to: The church in Philippi, a Roman colony
PHP.w: Philippi was proud of its Roman citizenship. Paul says the church's citizenship is in heaven.

COL.w: A mix of Jewish rules, angel worship and philosophy was being taught.

1TH.w: Converted only months before and persecuted, they worried about believers who had died.

2TH.w: Some claimed the day of the Lord had already come and stopped working.

1TI.by: Paul (many scholars say a later follower)
1TI.to: Timothy, leading the church in Ephesus
1TI.w: False teachers within the church. Instructions on leaders and widows.

2TI.w: Paul's last letter, written under Nero, expecting death.

TIT.w: Cretans had a reputation across the ancient world. Paul quotes one of their own poets.

PHM.to: Philemon, a slave-owner, and his house church
PHM.w: Onesimus, a runaway slave, had become a Christian. Paul sends him back "not now as a servant, but above a servant."

HEB.to: Jewish Christians tempted to turn back
HEB.w: The temple and its sacrifices were probably still running. The letter argues that Jesus is the greater priest and sacrifice.

JAS.to: "The twelve tribes scattered abroad", Jewish believers
JAS.w: Poor believers under rich landlords. Practical wisdom close to Jesus' Sermon on the Mount.

1PE.w: Christians were slandered as antisocial and atheists for refusing the gods. Peter calls them "strangers and pilgrims".

2PE.w: Scoffers asked where the promised return of Christ was.

1JN.to: Churches around Ephesus after a split
1JN.w: A group had left, denying Jesus had come in the flesh.

2JN.to: "The elect lady" (a church) and her children
2JN.w: Travelling teachers depended on hospitality. John warns not to host deceivers.

3JN.w: A local leader, Diotrephes, refused to receive John's messengers.

JUD.w: Quotes 1 Enoch and the Assumption of Moses, books well known to its readers.

REV.to: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia
REV.w: Emperor worship was spreading through Asia. Revelation uses the code of apocalypse: beasts, Babylon and numbers.
